territory.path: Latin territorium meant the land under a town's jurisdiction. Some scholars instead link it to terrere, 'to frighten' (land from which outsiders were warned off), but the earth sense prevailed in English usage as land or a sphere of activity.

terse.path: Latin tersus described polished, neat prose, wiped clean of excess. That sense narrowed to writing or speech free of superfluous words, brief and to the point.

testator.path: A testator formally 'testifies' to his wishes in a legal will, witnessing his own intentions for after death.

theory.path: Greek theoria meant contemplative looking, mental viewing of an idea. It came to mean a systematic explanation reached through reasoned contemplation, as opposed to raw practice.

thorough.path: A variant of 'through': to do something thorough is to go all the way through it, leaving nothing unexamined, complete and careful in every detail.

thoroughgoing.path: Same root as thorough: emphasizes completeness, going all the way through something without exception, absolute and complete.

thrall.path: Direct from the root: to be 'in thrall' to something is to be enslaved or controlled by it, as a thrall was bound to a master.

threadbare.path: Fabric worn threadbare has lost its nap, leaving only the base threads showing. The image extended to anything worn out or overused, like an excuse worn threadbare from repetition.

thrifty.path: Originally meant thriving or prospering. It narrowed to the careful management of resources that lets one thrive, hence careful with money.

throng.path: Direct from the root: a throng is a mass of people pressed tightly together.

thwart.path: To thwart someone originally meant to lie or go athwart, crosswise to their path, blocking it. The sense settled into preventing someone from succeeding.

tide.path: Originally simply meant 'time' (preserved in Christmastide). It narrowed to the sea's rise and fall, tied to fixed times, then extended figuratively to any powerful recurring trend or current.

timely.path: Direct from the root: happening at a suitable, fitting time.

timorous.path: Direct from the root: filled with fear, nervous and lacking confidence.

parts.meaning: to draw, pull, fire a shot

tirade.path: Italian tirata meant a volley of shots, a long pull or draw. It became a long, forceful outpouring of words, an angry speech fired off in a burst.

parts.meaning: a charlatan's assistant who ate a toad

toady.path: Traveling quack doctors kept an assistant who would swallow a (supposedly poisonous) toad so the charlatan could dramatically 'cure' him in public, proving the remedy's power. The assistant's abject submission gave us toady for a servile flatterer.

toil.path: Originally meant to argue or struggle contentiously. The sense shifted from verbal wrangling to strenuous physical labor, hard, exhausting work.

token.path: A token is a symbolic sign standing for something larger. As an adjective it describes an act done merely as a symbolic gesture, a minimal show rather than substantial effort.

tome.path: Long ancient texts were cut into sections or rolls (tomoi) for handling. Tome came to mean a large book, from the idea of a cut or divided volume of a larger work.

torpid.path: Direct from the root: physically numb or stiff, extended to sluggish and inactive generally.

torpor.path: Same root as torpid: a state of numb inactivity and lethargy.

torque.path: Direct from the root: a rotational, twisting force.

torrid.path: Originally described land scorched by heat, as in the 'torrid zone' near the equator. The image of burning extended figuratively to intense passion.

tortuous.path: Physically winding and twisted, extended to arguments or processes so full of turns that they become excessively complex and hard to follow.

tour.path: From the circular motion of a lathe came the sense of a circuit, a journey that visits several places and eventually turns back to the start.

tout.path: Originally meant to peer or spy out, as watching for customers. The sense developed into loudly soliciting attention for something, promoting it aggressively.

tract.path: An area of land is a stretch 'drawn out' over a distance; a written tract is likewise a piece drawn out at length on a serious subject.

tractable.path: Something tractable can be handled or led easily, like an animal that can be pulled along without resistance, hence easily managed or solved.

traduce.path: Latin traducere originally meant to lead someone across, as in a parade for public shame and ridicule. It came to mean speaking falsely and damagingly about someone.

tranquil.path: A direct borrowing meaning calm and still; the word's internal formation is uncertain, but its sense of undisturbed peace has stayed constant.

transcend.path: Direct from the parts: to transcend is to climb over or beyond ordinary limits.

transgression.path: To transgress is to step across a boundary or line, such as a law or rule; a transgression is that violation.

transient.path: Direct from the parts: something transient passes through and moves on, lasting only briefly.

transitory.path: Same root as transient: not permanent, passing through in time rather than lasting.

transmute.path: Direct from the parts: to change from one form into an entirely different one, as alchemists sought to transmute base metal into gold.

trappings.path: Originally the decorative cloth draped over a horse to display its owner's status. The word extended to any outward accessories or ornaments that signal rank.

travail.path: The presumed source is a Roman device of three stakes used to restrain or torture. The word for that suffering broadened into painful, laborious effort and labor pains.

travesty.path: Originally meant a comic work deliberately dressed up in a disguised, grotesque form to parody a serious original. It extended to any grotesque distortion of something.

treacherous.path: Direct from the root: describes disloyalty and deceit in a person, extended to anything dangerously unreliable, like treacherous terrain.

treacly.path: Treacle originally meant a medicinal antidote against venom, later a syrupy medicine and eventually molasses. Treacly describes something cloyingly sweet like syrup, sickly sentimental.

tread.path: Direct from the root: to walk or step, often carefully, as in treading lightly.

treatise.path: A treatise is a formal written work that 'treats' or handles a subject systematically and thoroughly.

trenchant.path: Direct from the root: physically cutting extended figuratively to speech or criticism that cuts sharply and effectively to the point.

trepidation.path: Direct from the root: a trembling, fearful anxiety about what may happen.

tribulation.path: A tribulum was a heavy sledge dragged over harvested grain to separate it from the husks. Tribulation applies that grinding, crushing pressure figuratively to great trouble or suffering.

tribunal.path: In Rome the tribunus represented a tribe or the people; the tribunal was his raised platform for judging, giving us the word for a body appointed to judge disputes.

trifling.path: A trifle was originally an idle jest or something of no serious value. Trifling describes something unimportant and trivial, not worth serious attention.

trite.path: Something used so often that it has been rubbed thin through overuse becomes trite, overused and lacking freshness.

triumvirate.path: In Rome a triumvirate was an official ruling body of three men sharing power. It extended to any ruling group of three.

trivial.literal: of a place where three roads meet
trivial.path: A trivium, where three roads met, was an ordinary public gathering spot. Things discussed there were common, everyday chatter, of little importance next to serious learned matters.
